posts.post_title: Induced (Reflexive) Ovulators
posts.post_content: Which of the following is/are induced (reflexive) ovulators?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above (Camel, Cat, Rabbit)

Induced (reflexive) ovulators are species in which ovulation is triggered by the mechanical stimulus of mating (coitus), not by an endogenous LH surge tied to a fixed cycle.

Induced vs Spontaneous Ovulators
  • Induced ovulators: Ovulation ONLY occurs after mating stimulus → LH surge triggered by coital stimulation → ovulation follows in 24–36 hours. Examples: Camel, Cat, Rabbit, Ferret, Mink, Llama
  • Spontaneous ovulators: Ovulation occurs automatically during estrus regardless of mating. Examples: Cattle, Buffalo, Mare, Sheep, Goat, Sow, Bitch
Significance for AI in Induced Ovulators
  • In induced ovulators, AI or hormonal injection (hCG/GnRH) must be used to trigger ovulation since natural mating is not occurring.
  • In camel AI programs, ovulation is induced with GnRH or hCG at the time of insemination.
Memory Tip

'Camels, Cats, and Rabbits need a trigger (CCR — must be Coitally Cued for Reproduction)'

posts.post_title: Metestrus Bleeding in Cattle – Hormone Involved
posts.post_content: Post-estrus bleeding (metestrus bleeding) in cattle occurs due to withdrawal of which hormone?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Estrogen

Metestrus (post-estrus) bleeding in cattle occurs 1–2 days after the end of estrus due to the sudden withdrawal of estrogen. During estrus, high estrogen levels cause vasodilation and increased capillary permeability in the uterine endometrium. When estrogen levels drop sharply after ovulation, these capillaries rupture and blood passes through the cervix as a small amount of blood-tinged mucus.

Clinical Significance
  • Metestrus bleeding in cows appears as a small amount of blood on the tail/perineum approximately 1–2 days after standing heat ends.
  • It confirms that the cow was in heat 24–48 hours earlier — useful for retrospective heat detection.
  • It does NOT indicate that the cow is in heat at the time of observation.
Comparison
  • Proestrus bleeding (Bitch): Due to high estrogen causing diapedesis — before heat.
  • Metestrus bleeding (Cattle): Due to estrogen withdrawal — after heat. ✔

posts.post_title: Sperm Reservoir in Cow, Ewe & Doe
posts.post_content: Sperm reservoir in cow, ewe & doe is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cervix

In the cow, ewe, and doe, the cervix acts as the primary sperm reservoir. After mating or AI, spermatozoa are stored in the cervical crypts (annular rings of the cervix) from where they are gradually released into the uterus and oviduct over time.

Sperm Reservoir by Species
  • Cow, ewe, doe: Cervix ✔
  • Sow: Utero-tubal junction
  • Mare & bitch: Oviduct (isthmus)
Cervix as Sperm Reservoir — Practical Importance
  • In cattle AI, semen is deposited at the utero-cervical junction (mid-cervix or cervico-uterine junction) — not past the cervix — because the cervical crypts serve as the reservoir.
  • The cervix filters abnormal spermatozoa and provides a sustained release of capacitated sperm toward the oviduct.
  • Annular rings (transverse folds) in the cervix of ruminants and she-camel are the structures forming the crypts.

posts.post_title: Origin of PMSG/eCG Hormone
posts.post_content: PMSG (or Equine Chorionic Gonadotropin/eCG) is secreted by the endometrial cups of the equine placenta and is a hormone of which origin?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Foetal origin

PMSG (eCG) is secreted by the endometrial cups of the equine placenta. Although the endometrial cups are located in the maternal uterine tissue, they are formed from foetal trophoblast cells that invade the endometrium around day 36–38 of pregnancy. Therefore, PMSG is considered a hormone of foetal origin.

Timeline of PMSG in Mares
  • Chorionic girdle forms at ~day 25 of pregnancy
  • Trophoblast cells invade the endometrium at ~day 36–38 forming endometrial cups
  • PMSG secretion begins from day 40, peaks at days 60–70, then declines
  • Detectable until day 120–150 of pregnancy
Detection Tests for PMSG
  • Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) test: Detects PMSG in serum of pregnant mare
  • Cuboni test: Detects estrogen in urine of pregnant mare

posts.post_title: Most Confirmatory Sign of Heat in Cow
posts.post_content: Most confirmatory sign of heat in cow is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Stand still on mounting (Standing reflex)

The most confirmatory (definitive) sign of estrus in the cow is the standing reflex (immobilization reflex) — the cow stands still and allows itself to be mounted by other cows or the bull. This is also known as standing heat or sexual immobilization reflex.

Other Signs of Estrus in Cattle (non-confirmatory)
  • Restlessness and increased activity
  • Bellowing/vocalization
  • Clear, mucoid vulvar discharge
  • Chin-resting on other cows
  • Swollen, reddened vulva
  • Decreased milk production
  • Tail-head hair ruffled (riding marks)
Why Standing Reflex is Confirmatory

Other signs can occur during pre-estrus or post-estrus. Only the standing reflex reliably indicates true peak estrus (mid-heat), which is the optimal time for insemination. This is why heat detection in cattle relies primarily on observing standing behavior.

posts.post_title: Age for Starting Bull Training for Semen Collection
posts.post_content: Bull training starts for semen collection at approximately what age?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 18 months

Bull training for semen collection typically begins at 18 months of age. By this age, bulls have reached sufficient sexual maturity to be trained to mount a phantom or teaser animal and ejaculate into an artificial vagina.

Bull Management Timeline for AI
  • Puberty: ~10–12 months (first sperm present)
  • Training begins: ~18 months
  • Regular semen collection: From ~2 years
  • Maximum semen output: 5–8 years
Factors Affecting Training Success
  • Exposure to teaser females in estrus
  • Presence of experienced bulls
  • Proper nutrition and housing
  • Quiet, stress-free environment during collection
  • Best semen quality is obtained in the morning before feeding, during winter season

posts.post_title: Earliest Sign of Pregnancy – Rectal Palpation in Cattle
posts.post_content: Earliest sign of pregnancy on per rectal palpation in adult cattle is:

_aimcq_options.text: Fully developed C.L. on one ovary

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fully developed C.L. on one ovary

The earliest sign of pregnancy on per rectal palpation in adult cattle is the presence of a fully developed Corpus Luteum (C.L.) on one ovary. This can be detected as early as 18–21 days post-breeding.

Why C.L. is the Earliest Sign
  • After ovulation and fertilization, the C.L. of pregnancy (Corpus Luteum verum) forms and persists — it does not regress as it would in a non-pregnant cycle.
  • A well-developed, persistent C.L. (soft, protruding, mushroom-like body) on rectal palpation strongly suggests pregnancy.
  • This is detectable BEFORE other signs like membrane slip or fremitus.
Timeline of Pregnancy Signs on Rectal Palpation in Cattle
  • 18–21 days: Fully developed, persistent C.L. on one ovary ✔ (earliest)
  • 35–40 days: Slippage of foetal membrane (membrane slip)
  • 70–80 days: Palpation of amniotic vesicle
  • 80–120 days: Fremitus (vibration of middle uterine artery)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Slippage of foetal membrane → appears at 35–40 days, not the earliest.
  • Palpation of amniotic vesicle → detected around 70–80 days.
  • Fremitus → middle uterine artery pulsation is felt at 80–120 days — relatively late sign.

posts.post_title: Maternal Recognition of Pregnancy in Sow
posts.post_content: Maternal recognition of pregnancy (MRP) in sow is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Embryonic estrogen

In the sow (pig), Maternal Recognition of Pregnancy (MRP) is mediated by estrogen produced by the embryo/conceptus around 11–12 days of pregnancy. This embryonic estrogen prevents luteolysis (regression of the corpus luteum) by redirecting PGF2α secretion from endocrine (into bloodstream → C.L. regression) to exocrine (into uterine lumen → local, no C.L. regression).

MRP by Species Summary
  • Cattle: Bovine Interferon-tau (bIFN-τ / bTP-1) — at 16–17 days
  • Sheep: Ovine Interferon-tau (oIFN-τ / oTP-1) — at 12–14 days
  • Pig: Embryonic estrogen — at 11–12 days ✔
  • Mare: Transuterine migration of conceptus — at 12–14 days
  • Human: hCG (human Chorionic Gonadotropin) — at 8–10 days
  • Bitch & Cat: MRP not required (C.L. lasts full gestation regardless)

posts.post_title: Sperm Reservoir in Sow
posts.post_content: Which of the following acts as sperm reservoir in sow?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Utero-tubal junction

In the sow (pig), the primary sperm reservoir is the utero-tubal junction (UTJ) — the junction between the uterine horn and the oviduct.

Why UTJ in Sow?
  • In the sow, AI semen is deposited directly into the uterus via a corkscrew-tipped catheter — spermatozoa bypass the cervix as a reservoir.
  • Spermatozoa travel through the long uterine horns and accumulate at the utero-tubal junction, which regulates their entry into the oviduct.
Sperm Reservoir Comparison
  • Cow, ewe, doe: Cervix
  • Sow: Utero-tubal junction ✔
  • Mare & bitch: Isthmus of oviduct
AI Method in Sow
  • Corkscrew pipette method — 50 ml semen deposited into the uterus (not cervix) on the 2nd day of heat.

posts.post_title: Test to Detect Estrogen in Urine of Pregnant Mare
posts.post_content: In case of pregnancy diagnosis in the mare, which test is used to detect estrogen in urine?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cuboni test

The Cuboni test is used to detect estrogen (specifically estrogens/conjugated estrogens) in the urine of a pregnant mare. It is a colorimetric test — the urine is treated with sulfuric acid and resorcinol; a positive result shows a green fluorescence under UV light.

Pregnancy Diagnosis Tests in Mare
  • Cuboni test: Detects estrogen in urine → positive from ~150 days of pregnancy
  • Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) test: Detects PMSG in serum → positive from ~40 days to ~120 days of pregnancy
  • Rectal palpation and ultrasonography: Most reliable and earliest physical methods
Casoni Test

The Casoni test is actually an intradermal skin test used for the diagnosis of Echinococcosis (hydatid disease) — it has nothing to do with pregnancy diagnosis.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1-c, 2-e, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d

The correct matching of heat signs with animals:

  • Homosexual behavior (mounting other cows): Cow — cows in heat actively mount other animals and allow themselves to be mounted
  • Frequent urination during heat: Buffalo — buffaloes show frequent urination as a characteristic estrus sign, in contrast to cows
  • Rhythmic erection of clitoris: Mare — mares show 'winking' (rhythmic exposure of the clitoris) when teased by a stallion
  • Pro-estrus bleeding: Bitch — bitches show vulvar bleeding (sanguineous discharge) during pro-estrus before actual estrus
  • Flehman's reaction: Bull — the bull curls its upper lip and sniffs the urine/vaginal secretions of a cow in heat (olfactory evaluation of pheromones/estrogens)
Note on Buffalo vs. Cow

Buffalo shows silent heat (subestrus) more commonly than cattle, making heat detection harder. Signs like frequent urination and tail lifting are important indicators in buffaloes.

posts.post_title: Age for Maximum Semen Output in Bull
posts.post_content: Age of bull for maximum semen output should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5–8 years

Bulls produce the maximum semen output (in terms of both volume and total sperm numbers) between the ages of 5 and 8 years. During this prime reproductive period, the seminiferous tubules are at peak functional capacity.

Bull Reproductive Lifespan Stages
  • Puberty: ~10–12 months (first spermatozoa)
  • Training for AI: ~18 months
  • Good semen quality: 2–3 years onwards
  • Peak/maximum semen output: 5–8 years
  • Declining semen quality: After 10 years (old-age degenerative changes)
Factors for Optimal Semen Collection
  • Season: Winter is best for semen quality in bulls
  • Time: Morning before feeding
  • Frequency: Regular collection (2–3 times per week)
  • Nutrition: Adequate protein, vitamins A and E, zinc and selenium

posts.post_title: Fremitus Detection – Days of Pregnancy in Cattle
posts.post_content: During pregnancy diagnosis in cattle by rectal palpation, the fremitus (palpation of middle uterine artery) is seen at:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 80–120 days of pregnancy

Fremitus refers to the palpable vibration (buzzing or thrill) felt in the middle uterine artery due to increased blood flow to the gravid horn during pregnancy. It is detected at 80–120 days of pregnancy in cattle.

What is Fremitus?
  • As the uterus enlarges and the fetus grows, blood flow through the uterine arteries greatly increases.
  • This turbulent blood flow creates a palpable vibration in the middle uterine artery — called fremitus.
  • It is a reliable confirmatory sign of pregnancy, especially after 80 days.
Rectal Palpation Timeline in Pregnant Cattle
  • 18–21 days: Persistent C.L. on one ovary
  • 35–40 days: Slippage of foetal membrane (membrane slip)
  • 70–80 days: Amniotic vesicle palpable
  • 80–120 days: Fremitus of middle uterine artery ✔
  • 150+ days: Foetal parts palpable
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 35–40 days → that is when membrane slip is detected.
  • 70–80 days → amniotic vesicle is palpated at this stage.
  • 140–160 days → foetal parts are palpable; fremitus starts earlier.

posts.post_title: Hormone for Uterine Mucosa Preparation for Implantation
posts.post_content: The hormone responsible for preparation of uterine mucosa for implantation is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Progesterone

Progesterone is the hormone responsible for preparing the uterine mucosa (endometrium) for implantation of the embryo. It transforms the proliferative endometrium (built up by estrogen) into a secretory state, rich in glycogen and nutrients necessary for embryo nourishment.

Role of Progesterone in Reproduction
  • Uterine preparation for implantation: Stimulates endometrial glands to secrete 'uterine milk' (histotrophe) for early embryo nutrition. ✔
  • Maintenance of pregnancy: Maintains uterine quiescence (prevents contractions) throughout gestation.
  • Suppresses further follicular development: Negative feedback on GnRH/LH — prevents new estrus cycles during pregnancy.
  • Cervical mucus: Causes thick, tenacious mucus plug (closes cervix during pregnancy).
Estrogen vs Progesterone in Uterus
  • Estrogen: Proliferative phase — endometrial growth, increased vascularity, duct growth in mammary gland.
  • Progesterone: Secretory phase — glandular development, implantation preparation, alveolar growth in mammary gland. ✔

posts.post_title: Secretions of Sertoli Cells
posts.post_content: Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), inhibin & androgen binding protein (ABP) are secreted by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sertoli cells

Sertoli cells (sustentacular/nurse cells) of the seminiferous tubules secrete Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH), Inhibin, and Androgen Binding Protein (ABP).

Functions of Sertoli Cell Secretions
  • AMH (Anti-Müllerian Hormone / Müllerian Inhibiting Substance — MIS): Secreted by Sertoli cells in the fetal testes — causes regression of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) duct in males during embryonic development. Without AMH, the Müllerian duct would develop into the female reproductive tract.
  • Inhibin: Glycoprotein that selectively inhibits FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary — negative feedback control of spermatogenesis rate.
  • Androgen Binding Protein (ABP): Binds testosterone within the seminiferous tubules — maintains high local testosterone concentration needed for spermatogenesis.
Leydig Cells (for contrast)
  • Leydig cells (interstitial cells) secrete testosterone — the primary male sex hormone.
  • Leydig cells = endocrine cells of the testes.
  • Sertoli cells = exocrine + paracrine support cells (nurse cells). ✔

posts.post_title: Test to Detect PMSG in Serum of Pregnant Mare
posts.post_content: Which of the following tests is used to detect PMSG in the serum of a pregnant mare?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) test

The Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) test is a biological test used to detect PMSG (eCG) in the blood/serum of a pregnant mare. In the test, the mare's serum is injected into immature female mice — if PMSG is present, it causes follicular development and ovulation in the test mice (indicating pregnancy in the mare).

Summary: Pregnancy Tests in Mare
  • Cuboni test: Detects estrogen in urine (from ~150 days gestation)
  • A-Z test: Detects PMSG in serum (from ~40–120 days gestation)
Diagnostic Window
  • PMSG is detectable in mare serum from day 40 to day 120–150 of pregnancy, so the A-Z test is useful during this period.
  • Beyond 150 days, estrogen-based tests (Cuboni) are more reliable.

posts.post_title: Seasonal Polyestrous Animals
posts.post_content: Which of the following are seasonal polyestrous animals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mare, Sheep, Buffalo, She-camel

Seasonal polyestrous animals show multiple estrous cycles but only during a specific season of the year (influenced by photoperiod/day length). The correct group is Mare, Sheep, Buffalo, and She-camel.

Classification of Animals Based on Estrous Pattern
  • Monoestrous: Bitch, wild animals (only one estrous cycle per year)
  • Polyestrous (non-seasonal): Cow, Sow, Goat (continuous cycling throughout the year)
  • Seasonal polyestrous — Long-day breeders: Mare, Cat (breed when days get longer — spring/summer)
  • Seasonal polyestrous — Short-day breeders: Sheep, Buffalo, She-camel, Goat (breed when days get shorter — autumn/winter)
Note

Goat is sometimes classified as polyestrous and sometimes as seasonal polyestrous (short-day breeder). In the context of this question, the answer focuses on the most classically seasonal polyestrous animals.

posts.post_title: Best Season for Sperm Production in Bull
posts.post_content: Best season for total sperm production in the bull is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Winter

Winter is the best season for total sperm production in bulls. Lower ambient temperatures during winter help maintain optimal scrotal/testicular temperature, which is critical for spermatogenesis (testes need to be 4–5°C below body temperature).

Effect of Season on Semen Quality
  • Winter: Best semen quality — high motility, concentration, and normal morphology
  • Summer: Worst semen quality — heat stress causes scrotal hyperthermia, disrupts spermatogenesis, increases abnormal sperm and reduces motility. High ambient temperature is the most common cause of seasonal infertility in bulls.
  • Autumn/Rainy: Intermediate quality
Heat Stress Effects on Semen
  • Heat stress causes degeneration of germinal epithelium of seminiferous tubules
  • Increased primary and secondary sperm abnormalities
  • Reduced sperm motility and concentration
  • Effects may persist for 6–8 weeks after heat stress episode (spermatogenesis cycle duration)

posts.post_title: Pregnancy Diagnosis Method in Small Ruminants
posts.post_content: The method of pregnancy diagnosis in small ruminants (sheep & goat) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Abdominal palpation

In small ruminants (sheep & goat), the standard method of pregnancy diagnosis is abdominal palpation — pressing the abdomen externally on the right flank/ventral area to feel the foetus.

Why Abdominal Palpation in Small Ruminants?
  • Sheep and goats are small animals; the rectum is too narrow and fragile for per-rectal palpation (risk of rectal tear).
  • Abdominal ballottement and palpation can detect foetal parts, especially from 60–90 days of pregnancy onward.
  • Ultrasonography (transrectal or transabdominal) is also increasingly used in sheep and goats for early detection.
Pregnancy Diagnosis Methods by Species
  • Cattle & Buffalo: Rectal palpation
  • Sheep & Goat: Abdominal palpation ✔
  • She-camel: Cocking of tail + rectal palpation
  • Mare: Cuboni test & Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) test
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Rectal palpation → used in cattle/buffalo, not small ruminants (anatomy too small).
  • Cuboni test → used for pregnancy diagnosis in mare (detects estrogens in urine).
  • Cocking of tail → sign used in she-camel, not sheep/goat.

posts.post_title: Hormone for Alveolar Growth of Mammary Gland
posts.post_content: The hormone responsible for the alveolar growth of the mammary gland is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Progesterone

Progesterone is responsible for the alveolar (lobulo-alveolar) growth of the mammary gland — the secretory alveoli that actually produce milk.

Mammary Gland Development — Hormonal Control
  • Duct system growth: Estrogen — stimulates growth and branching of the ductal system.
  • Alveolar (lobulo-alveolar) growth: Progesterone — stimulates development of secretory alveoli (milk-producing units). ✔
  • Milk secretion (lactogenesis): Prolactin — triggers actual milk synthesis after parturition.
  • Milk ejection (let-down): Oxytocin — released by suckling stimulus → smooth muscle contraction of myoepithelial cells → milk ejection.
Memory Tip

'Estrogen = ducts, Progesterone = alveoli (Producing units), Prolactin = production, Oxytocin = outflow'

posts.post_title: Endocrine Cells of Testes
posts.post_content: Endocrine cells of testes are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Leydig cells

Leydig cells (also called interstitial cells) are the endocrine cells of the testes. They are located in the interstitial spaces between the seminiferous tubules and secrete the male sex hormone testosterone under the influence of LH (Luteinizing Hormone).

Cell Types in the Testes
  • Leydig cells (Interstitial cells): Endocrine cells → secrete Testosterone
  • Sertoli cells (Sustentacular/Nurse cells): Exocrine/support cells → secrete AMH, Inhibin, ABP (Androgen Binding Protein); nourish developing spermatozoa
  • Germ cells: Give rise to spermatozoa through spermatogenesis
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Sertoli cells → These are the exocrine/support cells, not endocrine cells. They do not secrete hormones into the bloodstream like Leydig cells do.
  • Both → Only Leydig cells are the true endocrine cells (secreting testosterone into blood).

posts.post_title: Factor Determining Half-Life of Hormones
posts.post_content: The half-life of a hormone is directly proportional to its:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sialic acid content

The half-life of glycoprotein hormones (like FSH, LH, hCG, PMSG) is directly proportional to their sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) content. Sialic acid residues on the carbohydrate side chains of these glycoprotein hormones protect them from degradation by liver enzymes, thereby prolonging their circulating half-life.

Sialic Acid Content vs. Half-Life (Correct Order)
  • PMSG: Highest sialic acid → longest half-life (~6 days)
  • hCG: High sialic acid → ~11 hours
  • FSH: Moderate → ~170 minutes
  • LH: Low sialic acid → ~60 minutes
  • Oxytocin: Not a glycoprotein → shortest half-life (~2 minutes)
Practical Significance

The long half-life of PMSG (due to high sialic acid) is why a single injection can be used for superovulation. In contrast, LH's short half-life necessitates pulsatile or repeated administration for therapeutic purposes.

posts.post_title: Purpose of Riding Test in Sows
posts.post_content: The 'Riding test' in sows is used to detect:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Heat (Estrus)

The Riding test (also called the Back Pressure Test) in sows is used to detect estrus (heat). A sow in true heat will exhibit the standing reflex (Wehrenberg reflex) — it stands rigidly and immovably when a person applies back/flank pressure, mimicking a mounting boar.

How the Riding Test Works
  1. The handler approaches the sow from behind and presses both hands firmly on the sow's back/hindquarters.
  2. A sow in standing heat will stand stock-still (positive test = in heat).
  3. A sow not in heat will move away or show resistance (negative test).
Enhanced Detection with Boar Exposure

The riding test accuracy improves greatly when done in the presence of a boar or with boar pheromone sprays. The pheromone androstenone from boar submaxillary glands triggers the standing reflex in sows.

posts.post_title: Best Time for Semen Collection
posts.post_content: Semen collection should be done during which time for best results?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morning before feeding

The best time for semen collection from bulls is in the morning before feeding. The bull is well-rested after the night, the ambient temperature is cooler in the morning, and fasting briefly before collection helps prevent digestive discomfort during mounting activity.

Practical Protocol for Semen Collection
  • Timing: Morning before feeding
  • Season: Winter gives best quality
  • Method: Artificial vagina (AV) — most preferred method in bulls
  • False mounting: Allowing 2–3 false mounts before actual collection increases sperm concentration and libido-based quality.
  • Collection frequency: 2–3 times per week for optimum output
Types of Artificial Vagina (AV) for Bulls
  • Russian AV (most commonly used in bulls)
  • Danish model (for bulls)
  • Norwegian model (for boars)
  • Mississippi model (for stallions)

Why She-camel Shows This Sign
  • In the pregnant she-camel, increased progesterone levels and structural changes cause her to cock (raise and deflect) her tail — this prevents the male from mounting.
  • It is an inexpensive, non-invasive field observation method, particularly useful in camels where rectal palpation can also be used but requires skill.

  • Sheep & Goat: Abdominal palpation

  • Mare: Cuboni test & A-Z test

posts.post_title: Hormone for Duct System Growth of Mammary Gland
posts.post_content: The hormone responsible for the growth of the duct system of the mammary gland is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Estrogen

Estrogen is responsible for the growth and branching of the duct system (ductal growth) of the mammary gland.

Mammary Development Summary
  • Duct growth: Estrogen ✔
  • Alveolar (lobulo-alveolar) growth: Progesterone
  • Milk synthesis (lactogenesis): Prolactin (+ somatotropin, glucocorticoids)
  • Milk let-down (ejection): Oxytocin
Why This Matters Clinically
  • In dairy animals, understanding the hormonal control of mammary development helps explain why cows with reproductive disorders (anovulation, luteal cysts) that produce excess estrogen or progesterone may show abnormal udder development.
  • Exogenous estrogen treatment can be used to stimulate duct development in prepubertal heifers for induction of lactation.

posts.post_title: Exocrine Cells of Testes
posts.post_content: Exocrine cells of the testes are:

_aimcq_options.text: Both Sertoli cells and Germ cells

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both Sertoli cells and Germ cells

The exocrine cells of the testes include both Sertoli cells and Germ cells, as both are components of the seminiferous tubule and contribute to spermatogenesis — a process whose products (spermatozoa) are delivered via ducts (exocrine secretion).

Seminiferous Tubule Components
  • Germ cells: Undergo spermatogenesis → produce spermatozoa
  • Sertoli cells (Sustentacular/Nurse cells): Support, nourish and protect developing sperm; secrete AMH, Inhibin and ABP
Endocrine vs Exocrine of Testes
  • Endocrine: Leydig cells → secrete testosterone into blood
  • Exocrine: Sertoli + Germ cells → contribute to spermatozoa production and secretion through tubular system

posts.post_title: Correct Order of Half-Life of Hormones
posts.post_content: The correct order of half-life of hormones (longest to shortest) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: PMSG > hCG > FSH > LH > Oxytocin

The correct descending order of half-lives:

  • PMSG: ~6 days (longest — highest sialic acid content)
  • hCG: ~11 hours
  • FSH: ~170 minutes
  • LH: ~60 minutes
  • Oxytocin: ~2 minutes (shortest — a peptide, not glycoprotein)
Key Reasoning
  • PMSG and hCG are glycoprotein hormones with the highest sialic acid content, hence the longest half-lives.
  • FSH and LH are also glycoproteins but with lower sialic acid content.
  • Oxytocin is a small nonapeptide (9 amino acids) with no carbohydrate moiety, making it rapidly degraded by enzymes — hence its very short half-life.
Memory Aid

P-H-F-L-O: PMSG → hCG → FSH → LH → Oxytocin

posts.post_title: Term for a Cow Always in Heat
posts.post_content: A cow which is always in heat is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both Buller and Nymphomaniac

A cow that is continuously or persistently in heat (nymphomania) is known as both a 'Buller' and a 'Nymphomaniac'.

Cause of Nymphomania in Cattle
  • Most commonly caused by Cystic Ovarian Disease (COD) — specifically follicular cysts (cystic follicles that fail to ovulate and continue to secrete estrogen).
  • The persistent estrogen secretion from the unruptured cystic follicle causes continuous behavioral estrus.
Treatment of Nymphomania/COD
  • GnRH: Triggers LH release → ovulation of the cyst or luteinization
  • hCG: LH-like effect → luteinizes the follicular cyst
  • Progesterone: Negative feedback to reduce estrogen dominance
  • Manual rupture per rectum: Not recommended (risk of adhesions)

posts.post_title: Cuboni Test & A-Z Test – Species Used
posts.post_content: Cuboni test & Ascheim-Zondek test (A-Z test) are the methods of pregnancy diagnosis in:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mare

Both the Cuboni test and the Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) test are pregnancy diagnosis methods used specifically in the mare (horse).

Cuboni Test
  • Detects estrogens (specifically estrone sulfate) in the urine of pregnant mare.
  • Urine of pregnant mare from ~120 days onward contains high levels of equine estrogens produced by the feto-placental unit.
  • A fluorescence reaction (greenish fluorescence under UV light) confirms pregnancy.
Aschheim-Zondek (A-Z) Test
  • Detects PMSG (Pregnant Mare Serum Gonadotropin) — now called eCG (Equine Chorionic Gonadotropin) — in the serum of pregnant mare.
  • PMSG is produced by endometrial cups from about 40 to 120 days of pregnancy.
  • The A-Z test uses injection of the mare's serum into immature female mice; if ovarian follicles develop, PMSG is present → pregnancy confirmed.
Summary of Equine Pregnancy Diagnosis
  • Cuboni test → detects estrogen in urine ✔
  • A-Z test → detects PMSG in serum ✔
  • Both are specific to the mare.

posts.post_title: Function of Pampiniform Plexus
posts.post_content: The function of the pampiniform plexus of the testes is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thermoregulation

The pampiniform plexus is a network of veins that surround the testicular artery in the spermatic cord. Its primary function is thermoregulation — it acts as a counter-current heat exchange system to keep the testes at a temperature 4–5°C lower than body temperature, which is essential for normal spermatogenesis.

Mechanism
  • Warm arterial blood coming from the body core is cooled by the cooler venous blood returning from the testes.
  • This counter-current exchange maintains testicular temperature lower than body core temperature.
Clinical Significance
  • Failure of thermoregulation (e.g., cryptorchidism — undescended testes) leads to infertility due to impaired spermatogenesis at elevated temperatures.
  • Scrotal hernia, hydrocele or fever can also impair thermoregulation and affect fertility.

posts.post_title: Optimal Time for Cow Insemination (Standing Heat)
posts.post_content: Best time for inseminating a cow is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mid-heat (Standing heat)

The best time for insemination in the cow is at mid-heat, also called standing heat, which corresponds to 12–18 hours after the onset of estrus. At this point, the cow stands immobile when mounted — the most reliable and practically observable sign of heat.

Why Mid-Heat is Optimal
  • Ovulation occurs 12–14 hours AFTER the end of estrus in cattle.
  • Sperm need ~6–8 hours to capacitate and travel to the fertilization site (ampullary-isthmic junction).
  • Inseminating at mid-heat ensures capacitated sperm are waiting when the egg is released.
AM–PM Rule
  • Heat detected in the AM → inseminate in the PM of same day
  • Heat detected in the PM → inseminate the following AM

posts.post_title: Animals with Annular Rings in Cervix
posts.post_content: Annular rings are present in the cervix of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ruminants and She-camel

Annular rings (transverse ridges/folds in the cervical lumen) are a characteristic anatomical feature of the cervix in ruminants (cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat) and she-camels. These rings provide tight sealing of the uterus during pregnancy (cervical plug) and complicate deep cervical penetration during AI.

Cervical Anatomy Across Species
  • Ruminants + She-camel: Annular rings (transverse folds) — difficult to pass a catheter deeply
  • Sow: Spiral/corkscrew folds — requires spiral-tipped (corkscrew) AI pipette
  • Mare: Soft, easily dilated cervix — straightforward to pass
  • Bitch: Narrow, angled cervix — difficult to catheterize
Clinical Implication

The annular rings in ruminant cervices make deep intracervical and transcervical uterine AI technically challenging, which is why laparoscopic intrauterine AI is sometimes used in sheep for frozen semen.

posts.post_title: Hormone Initiating Ferguson’s Reflex
posts.post_content: Ferguson's reflex is initiated by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Oxytocin

Ferguson's reflex is a neuroendocrine positive feedback reflex initiated by oxytocin. During parturition (and during nursing), stretching/distension of the cervix and vagina sends afferent nerve impulses to the hypothalamus, causing release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which then causes stronger uterine contractions — this is the Ferguson reflex.

The Ferguson Reflex Mechanism
  1. Foetus descends → cervix/vagina stretches
  2. Stretch receptors send signals to hypothalamus via spinal cord
  3. Hypothalamus triggers release of oxytocin from posterior pituitary
  4. Oxytocin stimulates stronger myometrial contractions
  5. Stronger contractions push foetus further → more cervical stretch → more oxytocin → positive feedback loop
Clinical Importance

Understanding this reflex explains why oxytocin injections are used to induce/augment labour. Epidural anesthesia can block this reflex by interrupting the afferent nerve signals from the cervix.

posts.post_title: Rutting Period in Deer, Elephant & Camel
posts.post_content: Males of deer, elephant & camel show their sexual activity in certain months — this period is known as the Rutting period. Which months correspond to the Rutting period?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: November to March

The Rutting period (also called 'must' in camels and 'rut' in deer) is the seasonal sexual activity phase in males of certain species. In deer, elephant, and camel, this occurs from November to March.

Rutting Period Details
  • Camel (Must/Musth): Male camels in rut show exaggerated sexual behavior, foam at the mouth, inflate the dulla (soft palate sac), and become aggressive. Occurs in cooler winter months (Nov–Mar) aligning with the breeding season.
  • Deer: Males grow antlers and show aggressive, territorial behavior during the rut — corresponds to autumn/winter months in the Indian subcontinent (Nov–Mar).
  • Elephant (Musth): Bull elephants secrete temporal gland fluid and show heightened aggression and sexual behavior — also peaks Nov–Mar.
Clinical Significance
  • During musth/rut, male animals can be dangerous to handlers — this is practically important for veterinarians and animal keepers.
  • This period coincides with the breeding season of the respective females (short-day breeders), ensuring synchrony for conception.

posts.post_title: Secretions of Seminal Vesicles
posts.post_content: Prostaglandins, fructose & ascorbic acid are secreted by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Seminal vesicles

The seminal vesicles secrete prostaglandins, fructose, citric acid, ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), riboflavin, and other components. They contribute approximately 60% of total semen volume.

Functions of Seminal Vesicle Secretions
  • Fructose: The primary energy source for spermatozoa motility — sperms undergo fructolysis for ATP production.
  • Prostaglandins: Stimulate uterine contractions to aid sperm transport up the female reproductive tract.
  • Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C): Antioxidant — protects sperm from oxidative damage.
  • Citric acid: Osmotic regulation of seminal plasma.
Secretions of Other Accessory Glands
  • Prostate: Alkaline fluid — neutralizes vaginal acidity; provides sperm motility and fertility factors.
  • Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands: Clear, mucus-like fluid — lubricates urethra before ejaculation, flushes residual urine.
  • Ampullae (Stallion): Secrete ergothioneine.
Note

Seminal vesicles and bulbourethral glands are absent in the dog.

posts.post_title: Silent Heat & TTE – Species
posts.post_content: Silent heat & temporary teat engorgement (TTE) is commonly seen in:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Buffalo

Both silent heat (subestrus — estrus without visible behavioral signs) and Temporary Teat Engorgement (TTE) are commonly seen in the buffalo.

Silent Heat in Buffalo
  • A major reproductive problem in buffaloes — the cow cycles normally (ovulation occurs) but shows minimal or no behavioral signs of estrus.
  • This makes heat detection difficult and leads to missed inseminations.
  • Hormonal factors, nutritional deficiencies, and the nocturnal preference for expressing heat contribute to silent heat in buffaloes.
  • Buffaloes tend to show heat signs predominantly at night — another detection challenge.
Temporary Teat Engorgement (TTE)
  • TTE is the temporary enlargement/engorgement of the teats observed in buffalo around estrus — due to increased estrogen-mediated vasodilation of the udder.
  • It is a useful secondary sign of heat detection in buffaloes.

posts.post_title: Name for Upper Lip Curling Behaviour in Bull
posts.post_content: The curling of the upper lip and sniffing behaviour shown by the bull is known as:

Correct Answer: Flehman's reaction

The characteristic behaviour of a bull curling its upper lip (lip curling/retraction) while sniffing the urine or vaginal secretions of a cow is called Flehman's reaction (also spelled Flehmen response). This behaviour facilitates the transport of pheromones and olfactory chemicals to the vomeronasal organ (Jacobson's organ) for evaluation of the female's reproductive status.

  • Seen in: Bulls, stallions, rams, cats, horses, and many other mammals
  • Purpose: Olfactory evaluation of estrogen/pheromone content in female urine/secretions to determine if she is in heat
  • Mechanism: Upper lip is curled back → nostril is closed → air/volatiles are channeled to the vomeronasal organ (VNO) in the nasal septum

  • Ferguson's reflex: Oxytocin-mediated positive feedback during parturition and suckling
  • Flehman's reaction: Olfactory sexual behaviour for estrus detection

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above (Sheep, Buffalo, Camel)

Short-day breeders are stimulated to breed by decreasing day length (shortening photoperiod — autumn/winter). Sheep, buffalo, and camel are all short-day breeders.

Photoperiod Classification of Seasonal Breeders
  • Long-day breeders (increasing daylength stimulates breeding): Mare, Cat
  • Short-day breeders (decreasing daylength stimulates breeding): Sheep, Goat, Buffalo, Camel ✔
Mechanism
  • Melatonin (secreted by the pineal gland during darkness) is the key mediator.
  • Short-day breeders: high melatonin (long nights) → stimulates GnRH → breeding season begins.
  • Long-day breeders: low melatonin (short nights) → stimulates GnRH → breeding season begins.
Non-Seasonal (Polyestrous) Animals

Cow, sow, and bitch cycle throughout the year — they are not strictly seasonally controlled by photoperiod.

posts.post_title: Split Heat & Foal Heat – Species
posts.post_content: Split heat & foal heat is common in:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mare

Both split heat and foal heat are characteristic reproductive phenomena of the mare.

Split Heat (Double Ovulation)
  • Split heat in mares refers to an interrupted estrus — the mare shows signs of heat, then appears to go out of heat briefly, then comes back into heat, with ovulation occurring during the second part. This is due to FSH surges stimulating two follicular waves.
  • Mares have a higher incidence of double ovulation (~25%) compared to other species.
Foal Heat
  • The first postpartum estrus in the mare occurs very early — approximately 7–12 days after foaling — this is called the foal heat.
  • Mating during foal heat is possible but conception rates are lower due to incomplete uterine involution.
  • The second postpartum heat (30–35 days) has better conception rates.

posts.post_title: Stage of Estrous Cycle During Ovulation in Cattle
posts.post_content: In cattle, ovulation occurs in which stage of the estrous cycle?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Metestrus

In cattle, ovulation occurs approximately 12–14 hours after the END of estrus — which places it at the beginning of the metestrus stage. This is unique among domestic animals, as most other species ovulate during estrus.

Stages of the Estrous Cycle
  • Pro-estrus: Follicle growth, rising estrogen, uterine hyperemia — preparation for heat
  • Estrus (Heat): Peak estrogen, sexual receptivity, standing reflex — lasts 12–24 hours in cattle
  • Metestrus: Post-estrus phase — ovulation occurs here in cattle, CL begins to form; metestrus bleeding (due to estrogen withdrawal) may occur
  • Diestrus: Dominant progesterone phase, active CL, preparation of uterus for implantation
Practical Implication

Since ovulation occurs in metestrus (after estrus ends), inseminating mid-heat (standing heat) allows sperm to capacitate and reach the oviduct in time to meet the ovum upon ovulation in early metestrus.

posts.post_title: Characteristic of the Second Stage of Parturition
posts.post_content: The second stage of parturition is characterized by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Delivery of the newborn

The second stage of parturition is characterized by the actual delivery of the newborn (birth). It begins with full cervical dilation and complete rupture of the chorioallantois, and ends with expulsion of the foetus.

The Three Stages of Parturition
  • Stage 1 (Preparatory stage): Dilation of the cervix; beginning of uterine contractions; chorionic sac rupture; lasts 2–6 hours in cattle
  • Stage 2 (Expulsion stage): Delivery of the newborn ✔; strong abdominal straining; lasts 0.5–1 hour in cattle
  • Stage 3 (Cleansing stage): Expulsion of foetal membranes (placenta/afterbirth) + involution of uterus; lasts 6–12 hours in cattle
Retained Foetal Membranes (RFM)

If foetal membranes are not expelled within 12 hours in cattle (24 hours in mares), it is considered RFM — a common post-parturient complication requiring veterinary intervention.

  • 2. Os-penis → (d) Dog: Os-penis (baculum) is a heterotopic bone found in the penis of dogs (and other carnivores). It supports penile rigidity independently of blood engorgement.
  • 3. Wolffian duct (Mesonephric duct) → (c) Male genitalia: The Wolffian (mesonephric) duct differentiates into the male reproductive tract under testosterone influence — forming epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles.

posts.post_title: Length of Estrous Cycle in Ewe
posts.post_content: The length of the estrous cycle in ewe is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 17 days

The length of the estrous cycle (inter-estrus interval) in the ewe (female sheep) is 17 days.

Estrous Cycle vs Estrus Duration — Common Confusion
  • Estrous cycle = total length from one heat to the next heat (includes proestrus + estrus + metestrus + diestrus)
  • Estrus (heat period) = only the phase of sexual receptivity
Key Estrous Data for Ewe
  • Estrous cycle length: 17 days ✔
  • Estrus (heat) duration: 36 hours
  • Ovulation: occurs approximately 24–30 hours after onset of estrus
  • Seasonal polyestrous: short-day breeder (breeds in autumn-winter)
Comparative Table
  • Cattle: 21-day cycle, 12–24 hr heat
  • Sow: 21-day cycle, 2–2.5 day heat
  • Ewe: 17-day cycle, 36-hr heat ✔
  • Doe: 19-day cycle, 48-hr heat
  • Mare: 21-day cycle, 6-day heat

posts.post_title: Recommended Diluent for Bull Semen
posts.post_content: Recommended diluent in bull semen is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Yolk-citrate modification (Citrate-yolk extender)

The yolk-citrate modification (also called citrate-yolk extender) is the recommended diluent for bull semen in AI programs.

Components and Functions
  • Egg yolk: Provides lipoprotein and lecithin which protect sperm membranes from cold shock during cooling and freezing (cryoprotection).
  • Sodium citrate: Provides osmotic buffer and energy source; chelates calcium ions.
  • Glycerol (cryoprotectant): Added for frozen semen — penetrates sperm cells and prevents intracellular ice crystal formation.
Diluents by Species
  • Bull: Yolk-citrate modification ✔
  • Ram: Yolk-glucose citrate
  • Stallion: Glucose-gelatin
  • Boar: Yolk-glucose bicarbonate

posts.post_title: Best Time for Inseminating a Cow
posts.post_content: Best time for inseminating a cow is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mid-heat (Standing heat)

The best time to inseminate a cow is during mid-heat, also known as standing heat — when the cow stands immobile when mounted by another animal. This corresponds to 12–18 hours after the onset of estrus, which maximizes chances of conception.

AM–PM Rule
  • Cows detected in heat in the morning → inseminate in the evening of the same day.
  • Cows detected in heat in the evening → inseminate the next morning.
Why Mid-heat is Optimal
  • Ovulation in cattle occurs 12–14 hours AFTER the end of estrus (post-estrus ovulation).
  • Spermatozoa take 6–8 hours to capacitate and reach the fallopian tube.
  • Inseminating at mid-heat ensures capacitated sperm are already present at the ampullary-isthmic junction when ovulation occurs.

posts.post_title: Animal with Maximum Semen Volume Per Ejaculate
posts.post_content: Maximum volume of semen per ejaculate is seen in:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Boar

The Boar (male pig) produces the maximum semen volume per ejaculate among domestic mammals — approximately 200–250 ml per ejaculate. This large volume is due to the contribution of massive seminal vesicles (which also secrete inositol and ergothioneine) and bulbourethral glands.

Semen Volume Comparison
  • Boar: 200–250 ml (maximum)
  • Stallion: 125 ml
  • Bull: 5–8 ml
  • Ram: 1 ml (minimum)
Practical Implication
  • Because of the large semen volume in boars, the AI dose in sows is also 50 ml — the largest among all domestic animals.
  • In boars, a corkscrew/spiral pipette is used for AI to navigate the spiral cervix of the sow.

  • Fremitus (vibration of middle uterine artery): 80–120 days — the uterine artery becomes enlarged and shows a palpable vibration (thrill) due to increased blood flow

posts.post_title: Start of Foetal Period in Bovine Gestation
posts.post_content: In case of bovine gestation, the period of foetus starts from:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 45th day onward

In bovine (cattle) gestation, the period of the foetus begins from the 45th day of pregnancy onwards, and continues until birth. Before this, the conceptus is classified as an embryo.

Stages of Bovine Gestation
  • Period of Ovum: Fertilization to day 10–12 — the fertilized egg travels through the oviduct and arrives in the uterus
  • Period of Embryo: Day 13 to day 45 — organogenesis; the heart forms and starts beating on the 22nd day
  • Period of Foetus: Day 45 onward until birth — all major organ systems are formed; growth and differentiation continue
Why Day 45?

By day 45, all major organ systems are differentiated and the developing offspring transitions from an embryo to a foetus. This is the same transition used in human developmental biology (embryo → foetus at week 8–9 ≈ 56–63 days).

posts.post_title: Study of Male Reproductive System
posts.post_content: Study of the male reproductive system is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Andrology

Andrology is the branch of medicine and veterinary science that deals with the study of the male reproductive system — including testes, accessory glands, semen evaluation, and male infertility.

Key Terminology
  • Andrology: Study of male reproductive system ✔
  • Gynaecology: Study of female reproductive system
  • Theriogenology: The broader branch dealing with animal reproduction (both male and female) — includes obstetrics, AI, embryo transfer, reproductive disorders.
  • Reproductive Physiology: The study of physiological processes of reproduction — a broader concept, not specific to male or female.
Practical Importance of Andrology
  • Semen evaluation (motility, morphology, concentration) is an andrological procedure.
  • Breeding soundness examination (BSE) of bulls, rams, and stallions is andrological.
  • Infertility diagnosis in males is managed under andrology.

posts.post_title: Length of Estrus (Heat Period) in Ewe
posts.post_content: Length of estrus (heat period) in ewe is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 36 hours

The duration of estrus (heat period) in the ewe is 36 hours. This is the phase during which the ewe is sexually receptive and stands for mounting by the ram.

Important Distinction
  • Estrous cycle length (ewe): 17 days
  • Estrus (heat) duration (ewe): 36 hours ✔
Ovulation in Ewe
  • Ovulation occurs approximately 24–30 hours after onset of estrus — near the end of the heat period.
  • This is important for timing of AI — insemination 12–16 hours after heat detection gives optimal conception.
Heat Duration Comparison Table
  • Cattle: 12–24 hours
  • Mare: 6 days (longest)
  • Sow: 2–2.5 days
  • Ewe: 36 hours ✔
  • Doe: 48 hours
  • Bitch: 9 days

posts.post_title: Fertile Life Span of Spermatozoa in Mare & Bitch
posts.post_content: In domestic animals, fertile life span of spermatozoa in the female genital tract is 1–2 days. But in mare & bitch, the fertile life span of spermatozoa is about:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4–6 days

While in most domestic animals (cattle, sheep, etc.) the fertile life span of spermatozoa in the female genital tract is 1–2 days, in the mare and bitch it is extended to 4–6 days.

Why Longer in Mare and Bitch?
  • In the mare, sperm can be stored for longer periods in the uterine tube crypts and remain fertilizable for up to 4–6 days.
  • In the bitch, the unique ovulation timing (bitch ovulates primary oocytes, which then undergo 2–3 days of further maturation before fertilization is possible) means sperm must survive longer to ensure fertilization.
Fertile Life Span Summary
  • Most domestic animals (cattle, sheep, goat, sow): 1–2 days
  • Mare & Bitch: 4–6 days ✔
Compare: Fertile Life Span of Ova
  • Most domestic animals: 12–24 hours
  • Bitch: 4–8 days (ova remain fertile in oviduct for longer due to delayed maturation)

posts.post_title: Best Time for Inseminating a Sow
posts.post_content: Best time for inseminating a sow is:

_aimcq_options.text: Just before the end of heat

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2nd day of heat

In sows, the estrous cycle is 21 days and heat lasts 2–2.5 days. The best time for artificial insemination is the 2nd day of heat, as ovulation occurs around 35–45 hours after the onset of estrus, which aligns with the 2nd day.

Insemination Timing Across Species
  • Cow: Mid-heat (standing heat) or 12–18 h after onset
  • Sow: 2nd day of heat
  • Mare: Every 2nd day during estrus
  • Sheep (Ewe): 12–24 hours after onset of heat
Practical Tip

In sows, using the riding/back pressure test helps detect standing heat. The sow stands rigidly when back pressure is applied — this is the hallmark of true estrus in pigs.

posts.post_title: Site of Semen Deposition in Sow and Mare (AI)
posts.post_content: Site of deposition of semen in sow and mare during artificial insemination is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Uterus

In both the sow and the mare, semen is deposited directly into the uterus during artificial insemination. This is necessary because the cervix in these species does not act as an effective sperm reservoir (unlike in ruminants).

Site of Semen Deposition by Species
  • Cow: Utero-cervix (mid-cervix) — rectovaginal method
  • Ewe: Cervix — vaginal speculum method
  • Sow: Uterus — corkscrew pipette method
  • Mare: Uterus — vaginal/per-vaginal method
Why Uterine Deposition in Sow and Mare?
  • In sows, the cervix has spiral folds (interlocking ridges) that prevent deep penetration by a straight catheter — the corkscrew pipette locks into the cervix and delivers semen into the uterus.
  • In mares, the cervix is soft and easily traversed during estrus, allowing direct uterine deposition.

posts.post_title: Number of Spermatozoa from One Spermatogonium
posts.post_content: One spermatogonium produces how many spermatozoa?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 64

One spermatogonium undergoes multiple mitotic divisions followed by meiosis to ultimately produce 64 spermatozoa.

Steps of Spermatogenesis
  • 1 Spermatogonium → 16 Primary spermatocytes (4 mitotic divisions = 2⁴ = 16)
  • 16 Primary spermatocytes → 32 Secondary spermatocytes (Meiosis I)
  • 32 Secondary spermatocytes → 64 Spermatids (Meiosis II)
  • 64 Spermatids → 64 Spermatozoa (spermiogenesis — morphological maturation)
Summary Formula
  • 1 Spermatogonium → 16 Primary spermatocytes → 64 spermatozoa
  • 1 Primary spermatocyte → 4 spermatozoa
  • 1 Primary oocyte → 1 ovum (rest become polar bodies)

posts.post_title: Venereal Disease in Cattle
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a venereal disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both Vibriosis and Trichomoniasis

Both Vibriosis (Campylobacteriosis) and Trichomoniasis are classical venereal diseases in cattle — they are transmitted primarily through coitus (sexual intercourse) rather than through environmental contamination.

Vibriosis (Bovine Genital Campylobacteriosis)
  • Causative agent: Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis
  • Transmission: Venereal (coitus)
  • Effect: Early embryonic death, irregular return to estrus, infertility; occasional abortions
  • Prevention: AI with frozen semen can prevent transmission
Trichomoniasis
  • Causative agent: Tritrichomonas foetus (protozoan)
  • Transmission: Venereal (coitus)
  • Effect: Post-coital pyometra, abortion in 1st trimester, infertility
FMD vs. Venereal Diseases

FMD (Foot and Mouth Disease) is caused by an Aphthovirus and is transmitted via aerosols, contact with infected animals and fomites — NOT venereal.

posts.post_title: Type of Placenta in Bitch & Cat
posts.post_content: Type of placenta present in bitch & cat is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Endotheliochorial

The bitch (dog) and cat have a Zonary, Endotheliochorial type of placenta. In this type, the chorion is in direct contact with the endothelium of the maternal blood vessels.

Classification of Placenta by Histological Depth (Barriers)
  • Epitheliochorial (6 layers): Horse, pig, camel — chorion contacts maternal epithelium; least invasive.
  • Syndesmochorial (5 layers): Sheep & goat — maternal epithelium partially eroded.
  • Endotheliochorial (4 layers): Bitch, cat — maternal epithelium and connective tissue eroded; chorion contacts maternal endothelium. ✔
  • Haemochorial (3 layers): Human, monkey, rodents — most invasive; chorion bathes directly in maternal blood.
Classification by Shape
  • Diffuse: Horse, pig, camel
  • Cotyledonary: Ruminants
  • Zonary: Bitch, cat ✔
  • Discoid: Human, monkey, rodents
Memory Tip

"Zonary & Endotheliochorial = Zany (dog & cat are carnivores that are zone-shaped and eat endothelia)"

posts.post_title: Length of Estrous Cycle in She-Camel
posts.post_content: Length of estrous cycle in she-camel is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 23 days

The length of the estrous cycle in the she-camel is 23 days, with the heat (estrus) duration lasting approximately 3–5 days.

Unique Reproductive Features of She-Camel
  • Induced ovulator — ovulation occurs only after mating stimulus (coitus or GnRH injection).
  • Seasonal polyestrous — short-day breeder (breeds in cooler months, Nov–March).
  • Uterus: Bicornuate, shape between Y and T.
  • Gestation period: 390 days (longest among common domestic animals — approximately 13 months).
  • 99% of pregnancies are in the left horn.
Comparison of Estrous Cycle Lengths
  • Cattle, Mare, Sow: 21 days
  • She-camel: 23 days ✔
  • Doe: 19 days
  • Ewe: 17 days

posts.post_title: Fertile Life Span of Ova in Bitch
posts.post_content: The fertile life span of ovulated ova in domestic animals is 12–24 hours. But in case of the bitch, ova remain fertile in the oviduct for:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4–8 days

In the bitch, ovulated ova remain fertile in the oviduct for an exceptionally long period of 4–8 days — compared to 12–24 hours in most other domestic animals.

Why Ova Remain Fertile Longer in the Bitch
  • The bitch is unique in that she ovulates primary oocytes (not secondary oocytes like most other species).
  • After ovulation, these primary oocytes undergo first meiotic division (→ secondary oocyte) in the oviduct over 2–3 days.
  • Only after maturation to secondary oocyte stage can fertilization occur.
  • The combination of long maturation time + subsequent fertilization window = 4–8 day fertile lifespan.
Species That Ovulate Primary Oocytes
  • Bitch and mare — both ovulate primary oocytes (unique among domestic animals).
  • All other domestic animals ovulate secondary oocytes.

posts.post_title: Best Time of Insemination in the Mare
posts.post_content: Best time of insemination in the mare is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Every 2nd day during estrus

In mares, heat lasts for about 6 days and ovulation occurs 24–48 hours before the end of estrus. The recommended strategy is to inseminate every 2nd day during the entire estrus period to ensure spermatozoa are present at the time of ovulation.

Why Every 2nd Day?
  • Mares show a prolonged estrus (6 days), making it difficult to pinpoint exact ovulation timing.
  • Fertile lifespan of sperm in mares is 4–6 days (much longer than other species).
  • Inseminating every 48 hours ensures continuous coverage throughout the fertile window.
Additional Methods in Mares
  • Rectal palpation and ultrasonography can help detect the pre-ovulatory follicle (≥35 mm) to time insemination more precisely.
  • hCG injection can be used to induce ovulation and allow a single, timed insemination.

posts.post_title: Site of Semen Deposition in Cow and Ewe (AI)
posts.post_content: The site of deposition of semen in cow and ewe during artificial insemination is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cervix

In both the cow and the ewe, semen is deposited in the cervix during artificial insemination. The cervix in ruminants functions as the sperm reservoir, where spermatozoa are stored and capacitated before being released gradually into the uterus.

Important Distinction: Cow vs. Other Sources
  • For cows, the more specific site is the utero-cervix (mid-cervix) — semen is ideally deposited at the internal os of the cervix using the rectovaginal technique.
  • For ewes, vaginal speculum method deposits semen at the external os of the cervix (intracerivical), due to the complex folded anatomy of the ovine cervix.
Cervix as Sperm Reservoir in Ruminants

The cervical crypts harbor spermatozoa for up to 24 hours, releasing them gradually to compensate for the short ovum fertile lifespan. This buffering function is why cervical deposition is effective in ruminants.

posts.post_title: Number of Spermatozoa from One Primary Spermatocyte
posts.post_content: From one primary spermatocyte, how many spermatozoa are formed?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4

One primary spermatocyte undergoes Meiosis I to form 2 secondary spermatocytes, which then undergo Meiosis II to form 4 spermatids, which mature into 4 spermatozoa.

Pathway from Primary Spermatocyte
  • 1 Primary spermatocyte (2n) → Meiosis I → 2 Secondary spermatocytes (n)
  • 2 Secondary spermatocytes → Meiosis II → 4 Spermatids (n)
  • 4 Spermatids → Spermiogenesis → 4 Spermatozoa
Comparison with Oogenesis
  • 1 Primary spermatocyte → 4 functional spermatozoa
  • 1 Primary oocyte → 1 functional ovum + 3 polar bodies (wasted)
  • This contrast highlights the biological difference: males produce millions of sperm; females produce one mature egg per cycle.

posts.post_title: Causative Agent of Post-Coital Pyometra in Cattle
posts.post_content: Post-coital pyometra in cattle is caused by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trichomonas (Tritrichomonas foetus)

Post-coital pyometra in cattle (accumulation of pus in the uterus after mating) is caused by Tritrichomonas foetus, a protozoan parasite transmitted venereally during coitus.

Pathogenesis of Trichomoniasis
  • The protozoan is carried asymptomatically by bulls (in the preputial cavity) and is transmitted to cows during natural mating.
  • In cows: vaginal discharge → cervicitis → endometritis → pyometra ('potato soup' appearance of pus) → maceration of foetus if pregnant
  • Causes abortion in the 1st trimester of pregnancy
  • Bulls are carriers but rarely show clinical signs
Why Not the Other Options?
  • Leptospira: Causes abortion mainly in last trimester; not specifically post-coital pyometra
  • Listeria: Causes abortion in last trimester; mainly a foodborne pathogen (silage disease)
  • Campylobacter fetus: Causes early embryonic death and infertility, but characteristic feature is NOT pyometra; it is more associated with irregular estrus cycles and low conception rates

posts.post_title: Types of Placenta – Correct Matching
posts.post_content: Which of the following pair(s) regarding types of placenta is/are correctly matched?

_aimcq_options.text: Diffused placenta – mare, sow & she-camel only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

All three pairs are correctly matched:

  • Cotyledonary placenta → Ruminants (cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat): The placentomes (cotyledon + caruncle unit) are scattered over the chorion. Cattle have ~70–120 placentomes.
  • Zonary placenta → Carnivores (bitch, cat): The placenta forms a band/girdle (zone) around the middle of the chorion.
  • Diffused placenta → Mare, sow & she-camel: Chorionic villi are distributed all over the entire surface of the chorion (diffuse attachment).

posts.post_title: Duration of Heat (Estrus) in Mare
posts.post_content: Duration of heat (estrus) in mare is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 6 days

The duration of estrus (heat period) in the mare is approximately 6 days — the longest estrus duration among all common domestic animals.

Reproductive Data for Mare
  • Estrous cycle: 21 days
  • Estrus duration: 6 days ✔
  • Ovulation: occurs 1–2 days before end of estrus (day 4–5 of a 6-day heat)
  • Long-day breeder (seasonal polyestrous)
  • Uterus: T-shaped, bipartite type
  • Gestation period: 341 days (≈ 11 months + 11 days)
AI Timing in Mare

Because the mare has a 6-day heat with ovulation near the end, AI is recommended every 2 days during estrus — or once after confirmed ovulation by ultrasound.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 9 days → estrus duration of the bitch, not the mare.
  • 2 days and 4 days → do not correspond to any standard domestic animal.

posts.post_title: Timing of Ovulation in Cattle
posts.post_content: In all domestic animals, ovulation occurs during estrus. But in cattle, ovulation occurs:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 12–14 hours after end of estrus

In cattle, ovulation is a post-estrus event — it occurs approximately 12–14 hours after the end of estrus (approximately 28–32 hours after onset of standing heat). This is unique and clinically very important for AI timing.

Clinical Significance
  • Since ovulation occurs AFTER heat ends in cattle, inseminating during late heat or shortly after ensures sperm are present in the oviduct when the egg arrives.
  • The 'AM/PM rule' in cattle AI: if heat is seen in the AM → inseminate in PM; if heat is seen in the PM → inseminate next AM.
Ovulation Timing by Species
  • Most species (sheep, goat, sow, mare): Ovulation occurs during estrus (spontaneous, mid-to-late estrus).
  • Cattle: Ovulation occurs 12–14 hr AFTER end of estrus ✔
  • Bitch & Mare: Ovulate primary oocytes (not secondary oocytes).

posts.post_title: Storage Temperature of Frozen Semen
posts.post_content: Storage temperature of frozen semen using liquid nitrogen (LN₂) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: –196°C

Frozen semen is stored in liquid nitrogen (LN₂) at –196°C, which is the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. At this ultra-low temperature, all biological activity (including metabolism and enzymatic activity) is suspended, allowing virtually indefinite storage of spermatozoa.

Key Temperature Points in Semen Handling
  • Storage temperature: –196°C (in liquid nitrogen)
  • Dry ice temperature: –79°C (used for short-term semen transport)
  • Thawing temperature: 37–40°C for 30 seconds
Cryogenics in Semen Processing
  • Most commonly used cryogen: Liquid Nitrogen (LN₂)
  • Most commonly used cryoprotective agent: Glycerol (protects sperm from ice crystal damage during freezing)
  • Semen is typically processed into mini-straws (0.25 ml) or maxi-straws (0.5 ml) before freezing.

posts.post_title: Specific Site of Semen Deposition in Cow (AI)
posts.post_content: The site of semen deposition in a cow during artificial insemination is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Utero-cervix (mid-cervix)

In cows, the standard recommended site for semen deposition during AI is the utero-cervix — specifically at the internal os (cervico-uterine junction / mid-cervix). This is done using the rectovaginal technique where one hand is inserted rectally to guide the cervix onto the insemination pipette.

Rectovaginal Technique in Cows
  • The operator's arm is inserted into the rectum to palpate and stabilize the cervix.
  • The insemination pipette is guided through the vagina and advanced through the cervical canal to the internal os.
  • Semen is deposited at the utero-cervical junction for optimal results.
Why Utero-cervix and Not Uterus?
  • Deep uterine horn insemination is not routinely practiced in cattle.
  • The utero-cervical junction provides the best balance — it's deep enough to be close to where sperm travel up to the uterus, yet avoids potential uterine damage.

posts.post_title: Number of Ova from One Primary Oocyte
posts.post_content: How many ova are produced from one primary oocyte?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1

Only 1 functional ovum is produced from one primary oocyte. The meiotic divisions are unequal — while the genetic material divides equally, the cytoplasm is retained in one large cell (the ovum), and the other products become non-functional polar bodies.

Pathway of Oogenesis
  • 1 Primary oocyte (2n) → Meiosis I (unequal) → 1 Secondary oocyte (n) + 1st Polar body (n)
  • 1 Secondary oocyte → Meiosis II (unequal, triggered by fertilization) → 1 Ovum (n) + 2nd Polar body (n)
  • 1st Polar body may divide into 2 polar bodies
  • Net result: 1 Primary oocyte → 1 ovum + 3 polar bodies
Why Only 1 Ovum?

The asymmetric division conserves nutrients/cytoplasm in the ovum for embryo development. Polar bodies are anucleate remnants with minimal cytoplasm that degenerate.

posts.post_title: Most Common Cause of Abortion in Sheep & Goat
posts.post_content: Most common cause of abortion in sheep & goat is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Campylobacter fetus (Vibrio fetus)

The most common infectious cause of abortion in sheep & goat is Campylobacter fetus (previously known as Vibrio fetus), the causative agent of Vibriosis / Campylobacteriosis.

Campylobacter fetus Abortion
  • Causes epidemic abortion in ewes — often in the last trimester.
  • Spread venereally or through contaminated pasture/feed.
  • Two main subspecies: C. fetus subsp. fetus (intestinal tract) and C. fetus subsp. venerealis (venereal route in cattle).
  • In sheep and goats, C. fetus subsp. fetus is the primary cause of enzootic abortion.
Main Causes of Abortion by Species
  • Sheep & Goat: Campylobacter fetus ✔
  • Cattle: Brucella abortus
  • Bitch: Brucella canis
  • Swine: Leptospira
  • She-camel: Trypanosoma evansi
Important Note

Brucella, Leptospira, Mycobacterium, and Listeria cause abortion mainly in the last trimester, whereas Trichomonas foetus (cattle) causes abortion in the first trimester.

  • 2. Pseudo pregnancy → (c) Bitch: Pseudopregnancy (false pregnancy) is most commonly seen in the bitch after diestrus — elevated progesterone followed by prolactin rise causes mammary development, nesting behavior, and milk production without true pregnancy.
